question: A nautical mile is about 1,852 metres, noticeably longer than the land mile of about 1,609 metres. Why did sailors settle on this awkward length instead of simply borrowing the mile from land?
correct_answer: It equals one minute of latitude
alternative_answers: One sixtieth of a degree of latitude
Derived from degrees of the globe
So chart distances match latitude minutes
It matches the degree grid on sea charts
One minute of arc of a meridian
headline_answer: It equals one minute of latitude
source_excerpt: Historically, it was defined as the meridian arc length corresponding to one minute (1/60 of a degree) of latitude at the equator

extra.verification_notes: The nautical mile derives from one minute (1/60 degree) of latitude along a meridian, giving about 1,852 m; this was formally fixed at exactly 1,852 m in 1929 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nautical_mile).

explanation: The nautical mile was defined as the length of one minute of arc along a meridian, that is one sixtieth of a degree of latitude. Since sea charts are gridded in degrees and minutes, a navigator can measure a distance with dividers directly against the latitude scale on the chart's edge, with no conversion. The land mile has Roman origins unrelated to the globe, so it does not line up with the chart grid. Because the Earth is slightly flattened, the true length of a minute varies a little, so in 1929 the nautical mile was fixed by international agreement at exactly 1,852 metres.

question: The Scottish engineer who invented the unit 'horsepower' to market his steam engines later had an official unit of power named after himself. What is that unit?
source_excerpt: the SI unit of power, the watt, was named after him

extra.why_interesting: Players know horsepower and watts as rival units from car ads and light bulbs, but rarely connect that the same man is behind both names.
extra.verification_notes: James Watt, Scottish engineer, developed horsepower and the SI unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

explanation: James Watt compared his engines to horses to sell them, and today the watt, not the horsepower, is the official international unit of power.

question: Until 2019, which basic unit of measurement was officially defined by a single metal cylinder locked in a vault near Paris?
source_excerpt: The IPK and its six sister copies are stored at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in a controlled environment in a basement vault

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all units have been defined by physics for a century; in fact one base unit depended on a single lump of metal in a vault until very recently.
extra.verification_notes: The IPK, a Pt-Ir cylinder in a BIPM vault near Paris, defined the kilogram until the 2019 redefinition; the sister copies don't create ambiguity.

explanation: The platinum-iridium cylinder nicknamed Le Grand K was the kilogram for over a century, until the unit was redefined using a constant of nature in 2019.

question: The name December literally means 'tenth month', yet it is our twelfth. In which month did the early Roman year begin?
source_excerpt: It consisted of ten months, beginning in spring with March and leaving winter as an unassigned span of days before the next year.

extra.why_interesting: The names say 'tenth month' but December is the twelfth; the resolution is that the Roman year started two months later than ours.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Roman calendar article says the early Roman year began in March, consistent with the month names September to December.

explanation: The Roman year originally started in March, which is why September, October, November and December are named for seven, eight, nine and ten.

question: Which country stretches across five natural time zones yet keeps all its clocks set to a single official time?
source_excerpt: the largest sovereign nation in the world that officially observes only one time zone.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect huge countries to have many time zones like Russia or the USA; one giant country refuses, so the sun can rise at ten in the morning on its western edge.
extra.verification_notes: China spans almost five geographical time zones but officially uses only UTC+8 Beijing Time, and no change is reported (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_China).

explanation: The whole of China runs on Beijing time, so in the far west the sun can rise around ten in the morning by the clock.

question: The year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not. What is the next year ending in 00 that will be a leap year?
source_excerpt: Every year that is exactly divisible by four is a leap year, except for years that are exactly divisible by 100, but these centurial years are leap years if they are exactly divisible by 400.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every fourth year is a leap year; the stem reveals the exception and lets them work out the hidden rule.
extra.verification_notes: Gregorian rule makes centurial years leap only if divisible by 400, so after 2000 the next is 2400 (2100, 2200, 2300 are not leap years); source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_year

explanation: Century years skip the leap day unless they divide by 400, so 2100, 2200 and 2300 all miss out and 2400 is the next one.

question: In which country does the official calendar have thirteen months and show a year roughly seven years behind the one on most of the world's phones?
source_excerpt: the official state civil calendar of Ethiopia

extra.why_interesting: Players think of calendars as universal; one whole country is officially living in a different year with an extra month.
extra.verification_notes: Ethiopia's official civil calendar has 13 months and runs 7-8 years behind Gregorian (7 years from Sept 11 to Dec 31); Eritrea uses it only as a church calendar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_calendar).

explanation: Ethiopia uses its own ancient calendar with twelve months of thirty days plus a short thirteenth month, so its tourism slogan promises thirteen months of sunshine.

question: Diamonds are weighed in carats. Exactly how many milligrams is one carat?
source_excerpt: The carat (ct) is a unit of mass equal to 200 mg

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has heard of a one-carat diamond but almost nobody pictures how light that is: one fifth of a gram.
extra.verification_notes: The metric carat is defined as exactly 200 mg (adopted 1907) and has not changed, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carat_(mass).

explanation: A carat is one fifth of a gram, a standard that grew out of jewellers weighing gems against carob seeds.

question: Which unit of land area was originally defined as the amount a team of oxen could plough in a single day?
source_excerpt: the area of land that could be ploughed by one man using a team of eight oxen in one day

extra.why_interesting: Players treat the acre as an arbitrary number; it was actually a measure of a day's animal labour.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the acre was traditionally the area one man with a team of oxen could plough in a day; the jugerum is a minor rival but a 'yoke' is not a 'team'.

explanation: An acre was a day's ploughing for a yoke of oxen, which is why its old shape was a long narrow strip rather than a square.

question: True or false: when Anders Celsius first proposed his temperature scale, water boiled at zero degrees and froze at one hundred.
source_excerpt: 0 represented the boiling point of water, while 100 represented the freezing point of water.

extra.why_interesting: Zero for freezing feels like the only sensible choice, so players bet False and discover the inventor had it upside down.
extra.verification_notes: Celsius's original 1742 scale set 0 at water's boiling point and 100 at its freezing point, later inverted (Christin, 1743), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius

explanation: Celsius really did put boiling at zero and freezing at one hundred in 1742, and the scale was flipped to today's form shortly after his death.

question: The official second is defined by counting oscillations of a caesium atom. Roughly how many oscillations make one second?
source_excerpt: The caesium 133 atom's unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency is 9,192,631,770 when expressed in the unit Hz, which is equal to 1/s.

extra.why_interesting: Players know atomic clocks exist but have no feel for the scale; a single second is counted out in billions of atomic ticks.
extra.verification_notes: The SI second is defined as 9,192,631,770 caesium-133 hyperfine transition periods (~9.19 billion); redefinition cannot be ratified before 2030, so it still stands (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second).

explanation: A second is just over nine billion caesium oscillations, which is why atomic clocks lose less than a second over millions of years.

question: Thanks to its overseas territories scattered around the globe, which country observes more time zones than any other?
source_excerpt: France, including its overseas territories, has the most time zones with 12 (13 including its claim in Antarctica).

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Russia or the USA because of land size; the winner is a medium-sized European country whose islands circle the globe.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's list of time zones by country confirms France has the most (12, or 13 with its Antarctic claim), ahead of Russia and the US at 11 each.

explanation: France counts a dozen time zones from French Polynesia to New Caledonia, beating Russia and the United States, which each have eleven.

question: In 1712, one country officially had a 30th of February, to undo a botched attempt to change calendars. Which country?
source_excerpt: An extra day was added to February in the leap year of 1712, thus giving the month a unique 30-day (30 February) and the year a 367-day length.

extra.why_interesting: Players know February tops out at 29 days; one country once printed a 30th of February on its official calendar.
extra.verification_notes: Sweden added 30 February in 1712 to revert to the Julian calendar after its failed gradual Gregorian transition (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_calendar).

explanation: Sweden had drifted one day out of step with everyone else, so it added a second leap day in 1712 and briefly gave February thirty days.

question: Which country's national clocks are set five hours and forty-five minutes ahead of universal time, a quarter-hour offset shared by no other nation?
source_excerpt: Nepal Standard Time (UTC+05:45) is one of only three time zones with a 45-minute offset from UTC.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume clocks differ by whole hours, or at worst half hours like India; one country sits a quarter of an hour off everybody.
extra.verification_notes: Nepal uses UTC+05:45 nationally; the only other 45-minute offsets are sub-national (Chatham Islands, unofficial Eucla), so no other nation shares it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%2B05:45).

explanation: Nepal chose an offset based on the longitude of a mountain near Kathmandu, which leaves it fifteen minutes ahead of neighbouring India.

question: To reset the drifting Roman calendar, Julius Caesar made the year 46 BC extraordinarily long. How many days did it have?
source_excerpt: the longest calendar year in recorded history, lasted 445 days

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a year is always about 365 days; Caesar once stretched one to well over fourteen months to fix the drift.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 46 BC lasted 445 days, the longest year in recorded history, after Caesar added intercalary months before the Julian reform.

explanation: Caesar inserted extra months so 46 BC ran to 445 days, and Romans called it the year of confusion before the Julian calendar started in 45 BC.

question: Joe Woodland, co-inventor of the barcode, said the idea struck him on a Miami beach in the late 1940s when he dragged his fingers through the sand while thinking about which communication code?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: While at the beach, Woodland again considered the problem, recalling, from his Boy Scout training, how Morse code dots and dashes are used to send information electronically.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the barcode was a product of computer engineering; in fact its stripes are literally stretched-out Morse code drawn in beach sand.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Woodland drew on Morse code (dots and dashes) when he pulled his fingers through the sand at the beach in Florida circa 1948-49.

explanation: He drew the dots and dashes in the sand, then pulled his fingers downward and saw them become thick and thin lines, which is exactly what a barcode is.

question: Bananas are shipped green and turned yellow on schedule in sealed ripening rooms by pumping in a gas that the fruit also produces naturally. Which gas?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The room is gassed with ethylene, a naturally occurring gas emanated by ripening fruit, for 24 hours.

extra.why_interesting: Shoppers think yellow bananas simply ripened on the way over; in fact ripening is switched on deliberately, with a gas, to hit a shelf date.
extra.verification_notes: Commercial banana ripening rooms are gassed with ethylene, which the fruit also produces naturally; no contradicting or newer info found (https://theproducenews.com/choosing-right-banana-ripening-cycle).

explanation: Ethylene is the plant hormone that triggers ripening, which is also why a ripe banana in a fruit bowl hurries along the fruit beside it.

question: Crisp bags are puffed up with a gas that is not ordinary air. Which gas is used to keep the crisps from going stale and from being crushed?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The impact of nitrogen gas flushing on the stability of seasonings: volatile compounds and sensory perception of cheese & onion seasoned potato crisps

extra.why_interesting: The 'half-empty bag' is a running joke; the puff is actually a deliberate protective gas, and most people can reason their way to which one.
extra.verification_notes: Nitrogen flushing is the standard modified-atmosphere gas in crisp bags, displacing oxygen to prevent rancidity and cushioning against crushing; no contradicting or newer information found (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6148464/).

explanation: Nitrogen is cheap and inert, so unlike the oxygen in air it does not turn the frying oil rancid, and the cushion of gas protects the crisps in transit.

question: Fredric Baur, the engineer who designed a famous snack container in the 1960s, asked that some of his ashes be buried inside one. His family honoured the wish in 2008. Which snack?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Some of Baur's ashes were buried in a Pringles can at his request.

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a snack tube to be a burial urn; the player gets there by recalling which snack has a container famous enough to be its designer's pride.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Baur designed the Pringles can and some of his ashes were buried in a Pringles can after his death in 2008.

explanation: Baur was so proud of the stackable crisp tube that his children stopped at a shop on the way to the funeral home to buy the can, debating only which flavour.

question: In 1937 an Oklahoma grocer named Sylvan Goldman invented the shopping trolley by fixing two wire baskets to a wheeled version of which piece of everyday furniture?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: He found a wooden folding chair and put a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs.

extra.why_interesting: The trolley feels like it must always have existed; learning it began as a chair on wheels, and that shoppers initially refused to use it, reframes an invisible object.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Goldman's 1937 cart derived from a wooden folding chair fitted with wheels and baskets, then a frame holding two wire baskets.

explanation: Goldman's carts were based on a folding chair with baskets where the seat would be, and shoppers ignored them until he hired people to push them around the store looking happy.

question: Until 1916 a clerk fetched your groceries from behind a counter. That year Clarence Saunders opened the first self-service grocery store in Memphis, Tennessee, under which oddly animal-themed name?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Piggly Wiggly was the first self-service grocery store.

extra.why_interesting: Self-service shopping seems too basic to have an inventor, yet it has a date, a city and a deliberately silly name that still trades today.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly, the first self-service grocery, in Memphis in 1916; I found no newer development that changes this.

explanation: Saunders patented the self-service format and never properly explained the name, though he reportedly said he chose it so that people would ask exactly that question.

question: Despite its name, an ordinary tin can of beans is almost entirely made of which metal, with only a whisper-thin coating of actual tin?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Tinplate consists of sheets of steel coated with a thin layer of tin to impede rusting.

extra.why_interesting: The name says tin, and most people have never questioned it; the metal is almost entirely something else.
extra.verification_notes: Tin cans are tinplate, i.e. steel with a very thin tin coating (about 0.4–2.1 μm), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinplate.

explanation: The can is tinplate, a steel sheet with a tin layer thinner than a human hair to stop it rusting, which is also why a magnet sticks to it.

question: True or false: the small letter 'e' printed beside the weight on packaged food across Europe certifies that the quantity inside is exact.
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: the average quantity of product in a batch of prepackages shall not be less than the nominal quantity stated on the label

extra.why_interesting: Most shoppers have seen the little 'e' thousands of times and either ignored it or assumed it promises precision; it promises the opposite.
extra.verification_notes: The ℮ mark means the batch's average content is not below the nominal quantity, with permitted per-pack tolerances, so it does not certify an exact quantity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimated_sign).

explanation: The 'e' is the EU estimated sign, meaning the batch average meets the stated weight while individual packs may fall slightly under within set tolerances.

question: A chocolate bar left too long in a cupboard develops a dusty whitish coating that is often mistaken for mould. What does the confectionery trade call this harmless effect?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: Chocolate that has 'bloomed' is still safe to eat (as it is a non-perishable food due to its sugar content), but may have an unappetizing appearance and surface texture.

extra.why_interesting: Most people throw the bar away thinking it is mould; the trade has a gentle, almost poetic name for a completely safe effect.
extra.verification_notes: Chocolate bloom (fat or sugar bloom) is the standard trade term for the harmless whitish coating, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Fat bloom happens when cocoa butter migrates to the surface and recrystallises, and sugar bloom when moisture dissolves surface sugar; both are safe to eat.

question: Supermarket apples can be almost a year old, because growers keep them in sealed rooms where one gas in the air is cut from its normal 21 percent down to around 1 or 2 percent. Which gas?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: the normal 21% of O2 concentration of the air should be reduced to 1-3% by flushing the storage room with nitrogen gas

extra.why_interesting: Shoppers picture apples arriving from a recent harvest; many were picked a year ago and kept half-asleep in rooms where the air itself has been changed.
extra.verification_notes: Controlled-atmosphere apple storage lowers oxygen from 21% to about 1-3%, consistent with the claimed answer (https://extension.umd.edu/resource/controlled-atmosphere-storage-apples).

explanation: With almost no oxygen the apples barely breathe, so ripening nearly stops, and the rooms are so low in oxygen that workers must not enter them without ventilation.

question: In June 1974, a cashier in Troy, Ohio scanned the first barcode ever used at a supermarket checkout. The item cost 67 cents and a pack of it now sits in the Smithsonian. What kind of product was it?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The first retail scan of a product marked with a Universal Product Code was a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum that cost 67 cents.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the first scanned product to be something substantial like milk or cereal; it was a tiny impulse buy pulled from a cashier's basket to prove even small items could carry a barcode.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources confirm the first UPC scan on June 26, 1974 at Marsh in Troy, Ohio was a 67-cent 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, now at the Smithsonian (https://www.gs1.org/articles/marsh-holds-place-honor-history-gs1-barcode).

explanation: It was a multipack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit, chosen partly to show that a barcode could fit on something that small.

question: On the egg shelf, some eggs are white and some are brown. What one thing about the hen decides which shell colour she lays?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: The color of an egg is primarily determined by the chicken's genetics, and the breed of hen will usually indicate what egg color will be produced.

extra.why_interesting: Many shoppers believe brown eggs are more natural, organic or healthier, or that the colour comes from feed; in fact it is simply genetics, and the two are nutritionally the same.
extra.verification_notes: Eggshell colour is genetically determined and breed is the standard answer; earlobe colour is only a predictor with exceptions, so no clear error (see https://layinghens.hendrix-genetics.com/en/articles/eggshell-color-eggsplained/).

explanation: It has nothing to do with diet, freshness or farming method, and as a rough guide you can even predict it from the hen's earlobes: white earlobes, white eggs; red earlobes, brown eggs.

question: The Nutri-Score label, which grades a food from a green A down to a red E, now appears on packets across much of Europe. Which country invented it and adopted it first, in 2017?
topic: Supermarket science: packaging, labels and shopping
source_excerpt: adopted by the French Ministry of Health in early 2017.

extra.why_interesting: Because the label is so visible on German and Benelux shelves, players often guess Germany or the EU itself; the country famous for rich food and cheese is the one that invented the nutrition traffic light.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Nutri-Score was developed by Santé Publique France and France was first to adopt it in 2017; later adopters came in 2019-2021.

explanation: It was designed by France's public health agency and launched there in 2017, and Germany, Belgium, Spain and others only adopted it later, so despite the Germanic-looking name it is a French idea.

question: A former textile worker and hobby parachutist, which cosmonaut became the first woman in space in 1963?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: a textile factory worker and an amateur skydiver

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the first woman in space was a trained pilot or scientist from the 1980s; she was a Soviet textile worker and amateur parachutist flying alone in 1963.
extra.verification_notes: Tereshkova, a former textile factory worker and amateur skydiver, became the first woman in space on Vostok 6 on 16 June 1963 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentina_Tereshkova).

explanation: She orbited Earth 48 times alone aboard Vostok 6, and to this day she is still the only woman ever to fly a solo space mission.

question: Which researcher, watching a chimpanzee strip leaves from a twig to fish for termites in 1960, became the first to document a wild animal making a tool?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: tool creation by non-human animals had never been observed. Until then, tool making was considered one of the defining characteristics of being human.

extra.why_interesting: Tool-making was treated as the defining human trait; one young woman with no degree watching a chimp named David Greybeard overturned that in a single observation.
extra.verification_notes: Goodall observed David Greybeard modifying twigs to fish for termites in Nov 1960, the first documented tool-making by a non-human animal; no later development contradicts this (https://wiki.janegoodall.org/wiki/Tool_Making).

explanation: Her mentor Louis Leakey replied that science must now redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human.

question: Whose refusal to give up her seat on a city bus in Alabama in 1955 set off a boycott that lasted more than a year?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, for refusing to surrender her seat to a white passenger.

extra.why_interesting: A single quiet act on an ordinary evening commute set off a protest that lasted more than a year and launched the civil rights movement.
extra.verification_notes: Parks' Dec 1, 1955 arrest triggered the Montgomery bus boycott, which ran until Dec 20, 1956; Colvin's earlier refusal did not trigger it.

explanation: The Montgomery boycott ran for 381 days and ended only when the US Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional.

question: Which 1940s Hollywood star co-patented a frequency-hopping radio system for guiding torpedoes, an idea that underpins today's Wi-Fi and Bluetooth?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Lamarr co-invented a radio guidance system for Allied torpedoes that used spread spectrum and frequency hopping technology

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a glamorous 1940s film star and a radio engineer as two different people; here they are the same woman, and her idea is in every phone.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Lamarr co-invented (with George Antheil) the frequency-hopping torpedo guidance system, US patent 2,292,387 (1942); the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth link is a slight simplification but is commonly accepted.

explanation: Lamarr worked out the scheme with avant-garde composer George Antheil, who suggested synchronising the hops the way a player piano syncs its rolls.

question: The US Department of Defense named its standard programming language after which 19th-century woman, often called the first computer programmer?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: named after Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, usually known as Ada Lovelace

extra.why_interesting: Players know a Victorian countess is called the first programmer, but few connect her to a modern military language whose standard number is literally her birth year.
extra.verification_notes: Ada was developed under DoD contract and named after Ada Lovelace; the 1997 end of the mandate doesn't affect the past-tense 'named' claim (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ada_(programming_language)).

explanation: The language is simply called Ada, and the Pentagon gave its 1980 standard the number 1815, the year she was born.

question: Which future prime minister studied chemistry at Oxford under Dorothy Hodgkin, the Nobel laureate who worked out the structure of penicillin and vitamin B12?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Following her arrival at Oxford, Roberts began studies under X-ray crystallographer Dorothy Hodgkin, the tutor in chemistry for Somerville College since 1934.

extra.why_interesting: Players file prime ministers under law or politics, not laboratories; the Iron Lady was a research chemist trained by a Nobel laureate.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Thatcher (then Roberts) studied chemistry at Oxford under Dorothy Hodgkin, who supervised her thesis.

explanation: Thatcher worked as a research chemist before entering politics and kept a portrait of Hodgkin hanging in 10 Downing Street.

question: Before orbiting Earth in 1962, John Glenn refused to fly until which NASA mathematician had re-checked the computer's trajectory figures by hand?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Glenn had asked for her specifically and had refused to fly unless Johnson verified the calculations.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume NASA trusted its machines; the first American to orbit Earth trusted one woman's pencil arithmetic more than the computer.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Glenn refused to fly until Katherine Johnson verified the computer's calculations; no newer event affects this.

explanation: Her story was later told in the film Hidden Figures, and she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom at the age of 97.

question: True or false: Indira Gandhi, India's first female prime minister, was the daughter of Mahatma Gandhi.
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the Indian movement for independence from British rule

extra.why_interesting: The shared surname makes nearly everyone assume a family link to the Mahatma; the real political dynasty is the Nehru family.
extra.verification_notes: Indira Gandhi's father was Jawaharlal Nehru, not Mahatma Gandhi, so the statement is false and the claimed answer 'False' is correct.

explanation: Her father was Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, and the Gandhi name came from her husband Feroze, who was no relation to the Mahatma.

question: Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in 1431. In which year did the Catholic Church finally declare her a saint?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Canonized: 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a medieval martyr became a saint in the medieval era; it took the Church nearly five centuries, and the ceremony happened after the First World War.
extra.verification_notes: Joan of Arc was canonized on 16 May 1920 by Pope Benedict XV, per Wikipedia; 1456 was the rehabilitation trial, not canonization.

explanation: A retrial cleared her name in 1456, but sainthood only came in 1920, a few years after soldiers had carried her image through the trenches of the First World War.

question: Apart from the Curies, only one woman has a chemical element named in her honour. Which physicist, who first explained nuclear fission, is it?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: Unbinilium and Ubn are the temporary systematic IUPAC name and symbol respectively, which are used until the element is discovered, confirmed, and a permanent name is decided upon.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Curie has an element; they rarely know that the only other woman on the periodic table is the physicist who explained nuclear fission and was passed over for the Nobel.
extra.verification_notes: Meitnerium (element 109) honours Lise Meitner, and no new element has been named for a woman since; element 120 remains undiscovered per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unbinilium.

explanation: Element 109 is meitnerium, a belated tribute to the woman whose collaborator Otto Hahn alone received the Nobel Prize for the discovery of fission.

question: In 1960, which island nation became the first country in the world to be led by a female prime minister?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: the first woman in the world to be democratically elected prime minister in 1960.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Britain, Israel or India as the first country with a woman head of government; the real answer is a small island nation, years before any of them.
extra.verification_notes: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became PM of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in July 1960, the world's first female head of government; the 1960 name was Ceylon but Sri Lanka is the same country (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirimavo_Bandaranaike).

explanation: Sirimavo Bandaranaike took office in what was then called Ceylon, nine years before Golda Meir and almost two decades before Margaret Thatcher.

question: As a Cambridge PhD student in 1967, who noticed the regular radio pulses, jokingly nicknamed Little Green Men, that turned out to be the first known pulsar?
topic: Famous women in history and science
source_excerpt: The signal was temporarily dubbed 'Little Green Man 1' (LGM-1) before the source, now designated PSR B1919+21, was identified as a rapidly rotating neutron star.

extra.why_interesting: The signal was so regular the team half-joked about aliens; the student who found it in kilometres of chart paper was left out when the Nobel came.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Bell Burnell, as a Cambridge PhD student, detected the first pulsar signal in 1967 (LGM-1); no later events invalidate this.

explanation: The 1974 Nobel Prize for the discovery went to her supervisor Antony Hewish instead, a decision still cited as one of the great Nobel snubs.

question: The British monarch celebrates two birthdays every year: the real one, and an official one that is always held in June no matter when they were actually born. Why was the official birthday moved to summer?
correct_answer: Better weather for the outdoor parade
alternative_answers: Summer weather is better for the celebrations
The military parade needs fine weather
Trooping the Colour is held outdoors
Edward VII was born in November and wanted a summer celebration
Winter weather was too bad for the ceremony
headline_answer: Better weather for the outdoor parade
source_excerpt: Edward VII, who reigned from 1901 to 1910 and whose birthday was on 9 November, moved his official birthday to summer, in the hope of good weather.

extra.verification_notes: Edward VII (born 9 November) moved the official birthday to summer in hope of good weather, and the date is still in June under Charles III (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Official_Birthday_in_the_United_Kingdom).

explanation: The official birthday is marked by Trooping the Colour, a large military parade held outdoors in London. King Edward VII was born in November, and the British weather at that time of year was poor for a ceremony involving thousands of soldiers and crowds. In 1748 the parade had already been linked to the king's birthday under George II, and Edward VII made the June date permanent so the celebration could reliably take place in good weather. Queen Elizabeth II, born in April, and King Charles III, born in November, both kept the summer date for the same practical reason.

question: Which Oscar-winning Hollywood actress became Princess of Monaco when she married Prince Rainier in 1956?
source_excerpt: Grace Kelly married Prince Rainier III on April 19, 1956, becoming Princess of Monaco.

extra.why_interesting: A reigning Oscar winner walked away from Hollywood at the peak of her fame to marry into a tiny principality; the fairy-tale angle is real history.
extra.verification_notes: Grace Kelly won the 1955 Best Actress Oscar and married Prince Rainier III in April 1956, becoming Princess of Monaco.

explanation: Kelly retired from film at 26, just two years after winning her Oscar, and remained Princess of Monaco until her death in a car crash in 1982.

question: Henry VIII famously had six wives. How many of them did he have executed?
source_excerpt: At 8 am on 19 May 1536, Anne was executed on Tower Green.

extra.why_interesting: Players know Henry as the wife-killer, so many overestimate the body count; the rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died' gives the careful player a path to two.
extra.verification_notes: Anne Boleyn (1536) and Catherine Howard (1542) were the two wives Henry VIII had executed, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII).

explanation: Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard both went to the block, while the others were divorced, died in childbirth or outlived him.

question: Which European queen used her New Year's Eve speech in 2023 to announce she would abdicate two weeks later, after 52 years on the throne?
source_excerpt: Margrethe announced her abdication during her annual live broadcast address. The abdication took effect on January 14, 2024, marking exactly 52 years since her accession.

extra.why_interesting: European monarchs are expected to die in office, and Denmark had not seen a voluntary abdication in nearly 900 years; the surprise live-TV announcement made world news.
extra.verification_notes: Margrethe II announced abdication on 31 Dec 2023, effective 14 Jan 2024 after 52 years; no later events change this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margrethe_II).

explanation: Margrethe stepped down on 14 January 2024, the anniversary of her own accession, and her son became King Frederik X of Denmark the same day.

question: Catherine the Great, Russia's longest-reigning empress, was born in the Prussian port city of Stettin. In which present-day country is that city?
source_excerpt: in the city of Stettin (now known as Szczecin) within the Province of Pomerania in the Kingdom of Prussia.

extra.why_interesting: Players know she was German-born and the word 'Prussian' pushes them toward Germany, but the Baltic port is Polish today.
extra.verification_notes: Catherine was born in Stettin, now Szczecin, Poland; her 34-year reign is the longest of any Russian empress (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_the_Great).

explanation: Stettin became Szczecin when the border moved west after the Second World War, so the most famous Russian empress was born in what is now Poland.

question: What name did the British royal house carry until King George V replaced it with Windsor in 1917?
source_excerpt: Our House and Family shall be styled and known as the House and Family of Windsor.

extra.why_interesting: The most British-sounding of all names is barely a century old and was adopted to hide the family's German roots mid-war.
extra.verification_notes: The British royal house was Saxe-Coburg and Gotha until George V's 1917 proclamation adopted Windsor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Windsor).

explanation: The German name became a liability during the First World War, so George V rebranded the dynasty after Windsor Castle.

question: From 1890 until 2013, which European country was ruled by three queens in unbroken succession, without a single king?
source_excerpt: Wilhelmina 23 November 1890 – 4 September 1948; Juliana 1948 – 30 April 1980; Beatrix 1980 – 30 April 2013; Willem-Alexander 30 April 2013 – present

extra.why_interesting: Players assume monarchies are dominated by kings; here an entire country went 123 years without one, and the detail that the run ended in 2013 is a strong foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Wilhelmina (1890), Juliana, and Beatrix (to 2013) reigned consecutively before King Willem-Alexander; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_the_Netherlands

explanation: Wilhelmina, Juliana and Beatrix reigned one after another, so when Willem-Alexander took the throne in 2013 he was the first Dutch king in 123 years.

question: Which present-day US state was an independent kingdom with its own kings and queens until its monarchy was overthrown in 1893?
source_excerpt: the Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in a coup d'état

extra.why_interesting: Nobody pictures a US state with a royal palace, yet Honolulu still has one, and the kingdom fell within living memory of statehood.
extra.verification_notes: Hawaiian Kingdom was independent and its monarchy was overthrown on January 17, 1893; Hawaii is now a US state, and no other state fits.

explanation: Queen Liliuokalani was deposed by American business interests in 1893, and Iolani Palace in Honolulu remains the only royal palace on US soil.

question: Sweden's royal family, the Bernadottes, descends from a French marshal who had served which emperor before Sweden invited him to become crown prince?
source_excerpt: On 21 August 1810, Bernadotte was elected Crown Prince by the Riksdag of the Estates in Örebro.

extra.why_interesting: A French soldier from Napoleon's army ended up founding a Scandinavian dynasty that still reigns today; the French surname in the stem is the foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Bernadotte was a Marshal of the Empire under Napoleon, elected Swedish crown prince in 1810, and his House still reigns; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_XIV_John

explanation: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, one of Napoleon's marshals, was chosen as heir in 1810 and reigned as Charles XIV John, and his descendants still occupy the Swedish throne.

question: True or false: Queen Elizabeth II, one of the most widely travelled heads of state in history, never held a passport.
source_excerpt: Since all British passports are issued in the queen's name, she herself didn't need one.

extra.why_interesting: She was the most-travelled head of state in history, visiting well over a hundred countries, which makes the idea that she had no passport sound absurd until you hear the reason.
extra.verification_notes: Elizabeth II held no passport because British passports are issued in the monarch's name, so 'True' is correct; no newer events change this (see https://fortune.com/2017/04/21/queen-elizabeth-england-passport).

explanation: True. British passports are issued in the monarch's name, so the Queen needed none, though every other member of the royal family carries one.

question: Which of these British monarchs was never crowned?
source_excerpt: his reign from January 20 to December 11, 1936 ... abdication, with no coronation ceremony taking place

extra.why_interesting: All four are 20th and 21st-century British monarchs, so the solver must know that Edward VIII's reign ended before the ceremony that his brother then used, on the same date, for himself.
extra.verification_notes: Edward VIII abdicated in 1936 before his coronation; George VI (1937), Elizabeth II (1953) and Charles III (2023) were all crowned, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_VIII.

explanation: Edward VIII abdicated in December 1936 to marry Wallis Simpson, and the coronation booked for May 1937 went ahead on the same day for his brother, George VI.

question: In which year were Tsar Nicholas II and his family executed by the Bolsheviks?
source_excerpt: Nicholas II and his family were executed on 17 July 1918 at the Ipatiev House, Yekaterinburg, Russia

extra.why_interesting: Players fuse the abdication and the Revolution of 1917 with the killings, but the family lived in captivity for more than a year before being shot.
extra.verification_notes: Nicholas II and his family were executed on 17 July 1918 in Yekaterinburg, so 1918 is the only correct option; the date is not disputed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_II).

explanation: Nicholas abdicated in March 1917, but the family was held captive for sixteen months before being shot in a cellar in Yekaterinburg in July 1918.

question: Which country's king serves a five-year term, with the throne rotating among the hereditary rulers of nine of its states?
source_excerpt: Five years, renewable non-consecutively

extra.why_interesting: A king with a fixed term sounds like a contradiction; the clue about several hereditary rulers in one country narrows it to a federation with sultans.
extra.verification_notes: Malaysia's Yang di-Pertuan Agong serves a five-year term, elected from the rulers of nine states; no changes found as of 2026 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_di-Pertuan_Agong).

explanation: Malaysia's nine sultans and rajas take turns as national king, so the country gets a new monarch roughly every five years.

question: Born in May 1886, half a year after his father's death, which Spanish king was a reigning monarch from the moment of his birth?
source_excerpt: He became a monarch at birth as his father, Alfonso XII, had died the previous year.

extra.why_interesting: Players know of child kings, but a king from his very first breath is a different thing; the dates in the stem let a strong player reason toward the Spanish line of Alfonsos.
extra.verification_notes: Alfonso XIII was born 17 May 1886, six months after Alfonso XII died in November 1885, and was king from birth (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XIII).

explanation: Because his father Alfonso XII died while his mother was pregnant, the baby was proclaimed king the day he was born and reigned until Spain became a republic in 1931.

question: When Mary, Queen of Scots inherited the Scottish throne in December 1542, how old was she?
source_excerpt: Mary was born on 8 December 1542

extra.why_interesting: Most players know Mary as the adult rival of Elizabeth I and guess she was a teenager or young child at accession; six days old is the disbelief moment.
extra.verification_notes: Mary was born 8 Dec 1542 and succeeded on James V's death on 14 Dec 1542, making her six days old.

explanation: Her father James V died less than a week after her birth, making her one of the youngest monarchs in history, and she was crowned at nine months.

question: In a 1946 speech in the small town of Fulton, Missouri, which statesman declared that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe?
source_excerpt: From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an Iron Curtain has descended across the Continent.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the phrase but often assume it was coined by a Cold War president or a journalist; the surprise is that the Cold War's defining metaphor came from a British leader who had just lost an election, speaking in a small Missouri town.
extra.verification_notes: Churchill gave the 'Sinews of Peace' speech on 5 March 1946 at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, and used the 'Iron Curtain' phrase.

explanation: Churchill had just been voted out as prime minister, and his speech at a little college in Missouri gave the whole Cold War its most famous metaphor.

question: Laika, launched by the Soviet Union in November 1957, was the first living creature to orbit the Earth. What kind of animal was Laika?
source_excerpt: The Soviet Union and United States had previously sent animals only on sub-orbital flights

extra.why_interesting: Many players assume the first creature in orbit was a monkey or chimp because of the American programme; the Soviets actually sent a Moscow street dog, barely a month after the first satellite.
extra.verification_notes: Laika was a dog launched on Sputnik 2 on 3 Nov 1957 and was the first animal to orbit Earth; earlier animal flights were sub-orbital only (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laika).

explanation: Laika was a stray picked up on the streets of Moscow, chosen because street dogs were thought to be tougher, and she flew less than a month after Sputnik 1.

question: East Germany's secret police kept files on millions of its own citizens and recruited neighbours and even spouses as informants. By what short name was it known?
source_excerpt: the surveillance files that the Stasi had maintained on millions of East German citizens were declassified so that all citizens could inspect their personal files on request.

extra.why_interesting: The KGB gets all the attention, but the Stasi ran one of the densest surveillance states in history, with roughly one informant for every few dozen citizens.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Ministry for State Security (MfS) is commonly known by the short form Stasi, and describes its files on millions of citizens and spouse informants.

explanation: The Stasi built one of the most thorough surveillance states ever, and after 1989 Germans could request their own files and discover exactly who had informed on them.

question: In 1948 the Soviets cut every road, rail and canal link into West Berlin. For almost a year the Western allies kept two million people supplied anyway. How did the food and coal get in?
source_excerpt: Stalin ordered Soviet troops to block all rail and barge traffic in and out of Berlin.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a city of two million to need roads and rail; the idea that an entire city was fed, heated and kept alive for almost a year with planes landing every couple of minutes is still astonishing.
extra.verification_notes: Berlin Airlift supplied about 2 million West Berliners with food and coal by air during the 1948-49 Soviet blockade (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Blockade).

explanation: The Berlin Airlift flew in everything from flour to coal, with planes landing around the clock, until the Soviets gave up and lifted the blockade in May 1949.

question: The Berlin Wall famously came down in 1989. In which year did East Germany start building it, overnight and without warning?
source_excerpt: At midnight, the police and units of the East German army began to close the border and, by Sunday morning, 13 August, the border with West Berlin was closed.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows when the Wall fell, but most players assume it went up right after the war; it actually came 16 years later, in the same year humans first flew in space.
extra.verification_notes: Construction began overnight on 12-13 August 1961, per Wikipedia; no ambiguity or newer developments found.

explanation: Berliners woke on 13 August 1961 to find barbed wire splitting their streets, just four months after Gagarin had become the first human in space.

question: In October 1962 the world came closer to nuclear war than ever before over Soviet missiles in Cuba. The crisis lasted a specific number of days, later used as the title of a Hollywood film. How many days?
source_excerpt: The crisis lasted from 16 to 28 October 1962.

extra.why_interesting: The crisis looms so large that players imagine it dragged on for months; the whole brush with nuclear war fit inside two weeks, and the film title is a strong foothold.
extra.verification_notes: The crisis is conventionally dated 16–28 October 1962, which is 13 days, and the film is titled Thirteen Days (2000); the film link comes from general knowledge, not the fetched page.

explanation: From the day Kennedy saw the spy-plane photos to Khrushchev's announcement that the missiles would be removed was just 13 days, hence the 2000 film 'Thirteen Days'.

question: Kim Philby, Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean were senior British officials who secretly worked for Moscow for decades. Their spy ring was named after the university where they were recruited as students. Which university?
source_excerpt: All five were recruited by the NKVD at Cambridge University during the 1930s

extra.why_interesting: Players assume spies are recruited in back alleys and embassies; the most damaging Soviet moles in British intelligence were recruited as privileged students at an elite university.
extra.verification_notes: Philby, Burgess and Maclean were members of the Cambridge Five, recruited at Cambridge University in the 1930s (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Five).

explanation: The Cambridge Five were recruited by Soviet intelligence in the 1930s, and Philby rose so high he was once tipped to run MI6 while reporting everything to the KGB.

question: Spielberg's 2015 film 'Bridge of Spies' shows a Soviet agent being swapped on a Berlin bridge for an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960. Who was the pilot?
source_excerpt: the exchange of Powers and Abel is to take place at the Glienicke Bridge

extra.why_interesting: Players know a spy plane was shot down but often forget the pilot survived and became the centrepiece of the most famous prisoner swap of the Cold War.
extra.verification_notes: Powers, the U-2 pilot shot down in 1960, was exchanged for Rudolf Abel on the Glienicke Bridge, as the film depicts.

explanation: Powers was flying a U-2 spy plane at over 20 kilometres up when a missile brought him down, and the Soviets put him on trial before trading him for Rudolf Abel on the Glienicke Bridge.

question: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was a polished metal sphere with four antennas. Roughly how big was the sphere itself?

possible_answers.a: About the size of a tennis ball
possible_answers.b: About the size of a beach ball
possible_answers.c: About the size of a small car
possible_answers.d: About the size of a bus

correct_answer: About the size of a beach ball
source_excerpt: a 585-millimetre (23.0 in) diameter sphere

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the object that started the space race as something imposing; it was small enough to carry in your arms, which makes its impact on the world even more remarkable.
extra.verification_notes: Sputnik 1 was a 58.5 cm diameter sphere with two pairs of antennas, which is beach-ball sized; the other options are far too small or too large (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1).

explanation: Sputnik's sphere was about 58 centimetres across, roughly beach-ball size, yet its beeping signal was enough to send the United States into a panic and launch the space race.

question: True or false: when the famous Moscow–Washington 'hotline' was set up in 1963, it was a telephone line on which the two leaders could speak directly.
source_excerpt: Although in popular culture it is known as the 'red telephone', the hotline was never a telephone line, and no red phones were used.

extra.why_interesting: Films have cemented the image of a red telephone on the president's desk; the real hotline was a teleprinter sending typed messages, chosen deliberately to avoid misunderstandings in a live conversation.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1963 hotline was a teletype link, never a telephone line, so 'False' is correct.

explanation: The original hotline was a teleprinter link sending written messages, because both sides worried that a live phone call could lead to a misheard or badly translated word in a crisis.

question: Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space in 1963. In which year did the United States finally send its first woman into space?
source_excerpt: lifted off from the Kennedy Space Center (KSC) on June 18, 1983, Ride became the first American woman to fly in space, and the third woman overall.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Americans, having won the Moon, matched the Soviets on everything within a few years; the gap on this milestone was a full twenty years.
extra.verification_notes: Sally Ride became the first American woman in space on June 18, 1983 (STS-7), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride; this is a fixed historical fact and can't be superseded.

explanation: Sally Ride flew on the Space Shuttle in 1983, a full two decades after Tereshkova, and after the United States had already landed twelve men on the Moon.

question: In March 1965 a cosmonaut became the first person to float outside a spacecraft, and nearly died when his suit swelled so much he could not fit back through the hatch. Who was he?
source_excerpt: Leonov's spacesuit had inflated in the vacuum of space to the point where he could not re-enter the airlock.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to credit the Americans with every spacewalk milestone because of the Moon landings; the first person to float free outside a spacecraft was a Soviet cosmonaut whose suit nearly killed him.
extra.verification_notes: Alexei Leonov performed the first spacewalk on 18 March 1965 (Voskhod 2) and his suit ballooned so he could not re-enter the airlock, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Leonov had to let air out of his suit to squeeze back inside, and his twelve-minute walk beat the first American spacewalk by less than three months.

question: In 1961 Nikita Khrushchev sent the Kennedy family a puppy named Pushinka. Her mother, Strelka, was already world famous. What had Strelka done?
source_excerpt: had travelled into space aboard Korabl-Sputnik 2

extra.why_interesting: A gift of a puppy sounds like simple diplomacy; the twist is that the puppy's mother was a space traveller, making the gift a cheeky reminder of Soviet superiority in orbit.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Pushinka's mother Strelka flew into space aboard Korabl-Sputnik 2 and Pushinka was given to JFK in 1961.

explanation: Strelka and Belka orbited the Earth in 1960 and came back alive, so Khrushchev's gift was a living reminder that Soviet dogs had reached space before any American had.

question: In April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. What did he do at roughly 7 kilometres altitude on the way down that the Soviet Union kept secret for years?
source_excerpt: when Vostok 1 was still 7 km (23,000 ft) from the ground, the hatch of the spacecraft was released, and two seconds later Gagarin was ejected.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the first spaceflight ended with the hero touching down inside his spacecraft like every later mission; in fact the capsule hit the ground empty and the cover-up was about a rulebook, not safety.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Vostok 1 article confirms Gagarin ejected at ~7 km and parachuted separately, which the USSR officially denied until 1971.

explanation: The Vostok capsule landed too hard for a person inside, so Gagarin bailed out and came down under his own parachute. The Soviets hid this because aviation record rules required the pilot to land with the craft.

question: In 1945 Soviet schoolchildren gave the US ambassador in Moscow a carved wooden Great Seal of the United States. It hid a listening device that went undetected for seven years, designed by a Soviet inventor far better known for an electronic musical instrument played without touching it. Who was he?
source_excerpt: hung in the ambassador's Moscow residential study at Spaso House for seven years, until it was exposed in 1952.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the theremin as a spooky sci-fi instrument and never connect its inventor to espionage; the footholds (Soviet inventor, instrument played without touching) let a player reason their way to a name they already know.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1945 Young Pioneers gift to Harriman, the seven years undetected, and Leon Theremin as designer.

explanation: The device, nicknamed The Thing, needed no battery and was switched on by a radio beam from across the street. Theremin had built it while a prisoner in a Soviet research camp.

question: The marathon's awkward distance of 42.195 kilometres was fixed at which city's Olympic Games, where the course ran from a royal castle to the stadium?
source_excerpt: The modern 42.195 km (26.219 mi) standard distance for the marathon was set by the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) in May 1921 directly from the length used at the 1908 Summer Olympics in London.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the odd distance is ancient Greek; it is actually a British royal convenience from 1908.
extra.verification_notes: The 1908 London Olympic course from Windsor Castle to White City Stadium set the 42.195 km distance, which the IAAF formally standardised in 1921 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon).

explanation: At the 1908 Games the route began at Windsor Castle and ended in front of the royal box, and that 1908 distance later became the world standard.

question: At the 1960 Rome Olympics, Ethiopia's Abebe Bikila won the marathon in world-record time while doing without which basic piece of running equipment?
source_excerpt: In Rome, Abebe purchased new running shoes, but they did not fit well and gave him blisters. He consequently decided to run barefoot instead.

extra.why_interesting: A world record set without the one item every runner considers essential.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Bikila ran the 1960 Rome marathon barefoot and set a world record of 2:15:16.2.

explanation: Bikila ran the whole course barefoot over Rome's cobbles, becoming the first Black African Olympic champion, and won again in Tokyo four years later wearing shoes.

question: In which year did women run a marathon at the Olympic Games for the first time?
source_excerpt: the women's event was added to the programme at the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect women's marathon to have joined the Olympics decades earlier; it only arrived in 1984.
extra.verification_notes: Women's Olympic marathon debuted at the 1984 Los Angeles Games, per Wikipedia's Marathon at the Olympics page.

explanation: Women had to wait until the Los Angeles Games of 1984, where American Joan Benoit won, because officials had long claimed the distance was too dangerous for them.

question: In 2019 Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to cover the marathon distance in under two hours, in a European capital better known for waltzes and coffee houses. Which city?
source_excerpt: Kipchoge ran in Vienna, Austria on October 12, 2019, completing the marathon in 1:59:40.2.

extra.why_interesting: The historic run happened not in a famous marathon city but in a park in Vienna, chosen for its flat, sheltered course.
extra.verification_notes: Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna on 12 Oct 2019, the first sub-2 marathon distance; Sawe's later official sub-2 in London 2026 doesn't change that he was first.

explanation: Kipchoge clocked 1 hour 59 minutes 40 seconds on laps of Vienna's Prater park, though it does not count as an official record because of the rotating pacemakers and other help.

question: In 1967 Kathrine Switzer became the first woman to run which marathon with an official race number, despite an organiser trying to rip it off her mid-race?
source_excerpt: the first woman to run the Boston Marathon as an officially registered competitor

extra.why_interesting: The photographs of an official grabbing a runner are iconic, but many players do not know which race it was.
extra.verification_notes: Switzer was the first woman to officially enter and run the Boston Marathon with a bib (261) in 1967, and Jock Semple tried to remove it; Gibb ran unofficially without a number.

explanation: Official Jock Semple lunged at her a few kilometres in, but her boyfriend shoulder-charged him away and she finished; women were formally admitted to Boston in 1972.

question: The Ironman triathlon, which ends with a full marathon after a 3.8 kilometre swim and 180 kilometre bike ride, was first held in 1978 in which US state?
source_excerpt: The inaugural Ironman took place on February 18, 1978, in Oahu, Hawaii.

extra.why_interesting: The brutal format began as a bar-room argument between swimmers, cyclists and runners about who was fittest.
extra.verification_notes: The first Ironman was held on 18 February 1978 on Oahu, Hawaii, per Wikipedia; nothing newer changes this.

explanation: It started on the island of Oahu with just fifteen starters, settling a debate over whether swimmers, cyclists or runners were the fittest athletes.

question: The Comrades Marathon, held since 1921 over roughly 89 kilometres and regarded as the world's oldest and largest ultramarathon, takes place in which country?
source_excerpt: the world's largest and oldest ultramarathon race

extra.why_interesting: The biggest ultramarathon on Earth is not in the USA or Europe but in South Africa, and it predates most famous city marathons.
extra.verification_notes: Comrades Marathon is run in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa between Durban and Pietermaritzburg since 1921; ~88-90 km and 'world's largest and oldest ultramarathon' per Wikipedia.

explanation: It runs between Durban and Pietermaritzburg, switching direction each year between the uphill and downhill editions, and draws well over ten thousand runners.

question: The last-placed rider in the Tour de France is nicknamed the 'lanterne rouge'. That red lantern originally hung at the back of what?
alternative_answers: the last carriage of a train
source_excerpt: the red lantern hung on the rear vehicle of a passenger railway train or the brake van of a freight train

extra.why_interesting: Players know the nickname but rarely where the red lantern image comes from: railways, not cycling.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the lanterne rouge refers to the red lantern hung on the rear vehicle of a train, so the answer 'a train' is correct.

explanation: Railway workers used a red lantern on the final carriage to confirm the whole train had passed, so the cycling term means the man bringing up the rear.

question: Three of these cities host marathons in the prestigious World Marathon Majors series. Which one does not?
source_excerpt: Boston (1897), New York (1970), Berlin (1974), Chicago (1977), London (1981), Cape Town (1994), Sydney (2000), and Tokyo (2007).

extra.why_interesting: Paris hosts a huge, famous marathon, so players assume it belongs to the elite club; it has never been one of the Majors.
extra.verification_notes: Tokyo, Boston and Berlin are all World Marathon Majors; Paris is not a Major or a listed candidate as of Oct 2026 (Sydney and Cape Town were the recent additions).

explanation: Tokyo, Boston and Berlin are Majors alongside London, Chicago and New York, while Paris, despite one of the world's biggest fields, has never been admitted.

question: Which Belgian cyclist, winner of five Tours de France, was nicknamed 'The Cannibal' for his refusal to let rivals win anything?
source_excerpt: Merckx would not let anyone else win

extra.why_interesting: The nickname sounds brutal but simply described a rider who refused to leave any victory for anyone else.
extra.verification_notes: Merckx is Belgian, won the Tour five times (1969-72, 1974), and was nicknamed 'the Cannibal' for not letting others win; no newer event changes this.

explanation: Merckx won around 525 races in his career, including five Tours and five Giros, and the nickname reportedly came from a rival's young daughter.

question: At the chaotic 1904 Olympic marathon in St. Louis, winner Thomas Hicks was kept going by handlers feeding him brandy and small doses of which substance, better known as a rat poison?
source_excerpt: Hicks received several doses of strychnine – a common rat poison, which stimulates the nervous system in small doses – mixed with brandy and egg white.

extra.why_interesting: The first documented doping case at the Olympics involved an actual poison, and the winner nearly died on the track.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hicks was given doses of strychnine (a common rat poison) mixed with brandy and egg white; he remains the official winner despite Genty's petition.

explanation: In tiny amounts strychnine was then thought to be a stimulant; Hicks collapsed after finishing, and the first man across the line, Fred Lorz, was disqualified for riding part of the way in a car.

question: Thanks to its pancake-flat course, which city's marathon has produced more men's world records than any other, including Eliud Kipchoge's records of 2018 and 2022?
source_excerpt: Kipchoge 2:01:39 (September 16, 2018, Berlin Marathon); 2:01:09 (September 25, 2022, Berlin Marathon)

extra.why_interesting: Players guess London or Boston for records, but the record factory is the flat, cool-weather German course.
extra.verification_notes: Berlin has hosted about 12 men's marathon world records, far more than any other city; the 2026 London record by Sawe doesn't change that (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression).

explanation: Berlin's flat, wide roads and cool late-September weather have hosted a string of men's world records since the late 1990s, with Kipchoge running 2 hours 1 minute 9 seconds there in 2022.

question: The Tour de France was created by a sports newspaper as a stunt to boost its circulation. In which year did the very first edition roll out of Paris?
source_excerpt: The race was first organized in 1903 to increase sales for the newspaper L'Auto.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to date the Tour either to the late 19th-century bicycle craze or to the interwar years; it actually began in 1903, before cars had replaced horses on most French roads, as a newspaper's circulation stunt.
extra.verification_notes: The first Tour de France was in 1903, organised by L'Auto to boost sales (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tour_de_France); the start was in Montgeron, just outside Paris, which is a minor wording quibble.

explanation: The newspaper L'Auto launched the race in 1903 to beat a rival paper, and it worked so well that the leader's jersey later took the yellow colour of L'Auto's own pages.

question: However a badminton shuttlecock leaves the racket, even tumbling or struck at an odd angle, within a fraction of a second it is flying cork-first and stays that way. What about its design makes this happen?
correct_answer: Heavy cork in front, feather drag behind
alternative_answers: Weight at the front, air resistance at the back
Centre of mass is in the cork, drag is in the feathers
It works like an arrow or a dart: nose heavy, tail draggy
The feathers act as a stabilising skirt behind the heavy cork
headline_answer: Heavy cork in front, feather drag behind
source_excerpt: Regardless of initial orientation, it will turn to fly cork first, and remain in the cork-first orientation.

extra.verification_notes: The shuttlecock's heavy cork base and high-drag feather skirt make it aerodynamically stable and self-orienting cork-first, matching the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttlecock).

explanation: The cork base is far heavier than the feather skirt, so the shuttle's centre of mass sits right at the front. The wide cone of feathers, meanwhile, produces most of the air resistance, and that drag acts behind the centre of mass. Whenever the shuttle is sideways, the air pushes the light, draggy tail back behind the heavy nose, exactly like the fletching on an arrow or the flights on a dart. The effect is so strong that the shuttle self-corrects almost instantly, which is why badminton players can hit it from any angle without it ever arriving feathers-first.

question: The longest tennis match ever played was a first-round match between John Isner and Nicolas Mahut at Wimbledon in 2010. Over how many days was it played?
source_excerpt: 11 hours and 5 minutes over three days.

extra.why_interesting: Players know it was 'the longest match ever' but picture one very long afternoon; the answer reveals the match outlived the days it was scheduled in.
extra.verification_notes: Isner–Mahut (2010) was played over three days (22–24 June) and remains the longest tennis match; no longer match has been recorded.

explanation: Play was suspended for darkness twice, and the fifth set alone finished 70 games to 68, taking longer than any complete match before it.

question: In golf, one under par on a hole is a birdie and two under is an eagle. What is the name for the far rarer score of three under par?
source_excerpt: A hole played three strokes under par. Also albatross.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has heard 'birdie' and 'eagle'; the stem gives the ladder and the player has to reach for the rare top rung, which is a big seabird.
extra.verification_notes: Albatross is a standard term for three under par; 'double eagle' is a synonym, so accept both.

explanation: It is also called a double eagle in America, and it is rarer than a hole-in-one because it almost always needs a holed second shot on a par five.

question: In 1971, during the Apollo 14 mission, which astronaut became the only person ever to hit golf balls on the Moon?
source_excerpt: Shepard struck two golf balls, driving the second, as he jokingly put it, 'miles and miles and miles'.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes astronauts were all business; the answer is a man who smuggled a club head into his spacesuit pocket, and it is the first American in space.
extra.verification_notes: Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14 (Feb 1971), and no one has done so since; no crewed lunar landing has occurred since 1972.

explanation: Shepard, the first American in space, swung one-handed in his stiff suit and joked that the second ball went for 'miles and miles' in the low gravity.

question: The fastest recorded tennis serve is roughly 263 kilometres per hour. Which racket sport beats that comfortably, with smashes officially clocked at over 400 kilometres per hour?
source_excerpt: India's Satwiksairaj Rankireddy broke a decade-old Guinness world record for the fastest shot ever in badminton with an astonishing 565 km/hour smash.

extra.why_interesting: The player reaches for tennis or squash as the 'fast' sport; the gentle garden game turns out to launch the fastest projectile in all racket sports.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness-recognised badminton smash records are 565 km/h (Rankireddy, 2023) and 438 km/h (women's), both over 400 km/h, and the tennis serve record of ~263 km/h still stands.

explanation: The shuttlecock leaves the racket at extreme speed but its feathers brake it almost instantly, which is why rallies are still playable.

question: Tennis balls were traditionally white. Yellow balls were introduced to help television viewers follow the ball, but tradition-bound Wimbledon only adopted them in which year?
source_excerpt: Tennis balls of the 'optic yellow' colour were not introduced into Wimbledon until 1986.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume yellow balls have 'always' been standard, or guess the 1970s when colour TV arrived; Wimbledon held out until well into the 1980s.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources say Wimbledon first used optic yellow balls in 1986, although the ITF approved yellow in 1972; I did not open the Wikipedia page.

explanation: The international federation approved yellow balls in 1972, but Wimbledon kept white ones for another fourteen years before giving in.

question: In the year 2000, which sport made its ball two millimetres bigger, from 38 to 40 millimetres, deliberately slowing the game so spectators and television cameras could keep up?
source_excerpt: more viable as a televised spectator sport

extra.why_interesting: A sport deliberately handicapping its own ball sounds absurd until you realise the rallies had become too fast for cameras and spectators.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the ITTF changed the ball from 38mm to 40mm in October 2000 to slow the game for TV viewers, and the size has not changed since.

explanation: The larger, slower ball was introduced just after the Sydney Olympics, and the sport later also switched from celluloid to plastic balls.

question: Three of golf's four major championships move between different courses each year. Which major is always played at the same course?
source_excerpt: Unlike the other major tournaments which change host venues with each tournament, the Masters is always held at the same host venue: Augusta National Golf Club

extra.why_interesting: The stem's footholds let any casual fan reason it out: the one major with a permanent home is also the one with the famous green jacket.
extra.verification_notes: The Masters is always held at Augusta National, unlike the other three men's majors, which rotate venues (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Tournament).

explanation: It has been held at Augusta National in Georgia since 1934, which is why its azaleas and the winner's green jacket are so instantly recognisable.

question: Despite decades of campaigning, squash has never been an Olympic sport. At which Games will it finally make its Olympic debut?
source_excerpt: The 2028 Summer Olympics will include the sport of squash for the first time as an optional sport.

extra.why_interesting: A sport with a century-old professional circuit and world championships never made the Olympics; the player has to work out which upcoming Games finally lets it in.
extra.verification_notes: Squash is confirmed for its Olympic debut at LA 2028 (men's and women's singles, July 15-24, 2028) and has never been in the Games before, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squash_at_the_2028_Summer_Olympics

explanation: The International Olympic Committee approved squash in 2023 alongside cricket, lacrosse and flag football for the Los Angeles programme.

question: Only one tennis player in history has won all four Grand Slam singles titles and Olympic gold in the same calendar year. Who did it in 1988?
source_excerpt: German tennis player Steffi Graf achieved what no one else had done before or has done since.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Serena Williams, Federer or Djokovic as the greatest ever, yet none of them managed this; the answer is a teenager from 1988.
extra.verification_notes: Graf remains the only player to win all four Slams plus Olympic gold in one calendar year (1988); no Olympics since could have changed this.

explanation: Graf was just 19, and 1988 was the first time tennis had returned as a full Olympic sport since 1924, so the chance did not even exist for earlier champions.

question: Padel, the enclosed-court racket sport booming across Europe, was invented in 1969 by a man who built a court at his holiday home. In which country?
source_excerpt: Corcuera modified his squash court to incorporate elements of platform tennis.

extra.why_interesting: Padel is so dominated by Spain and Argentina that almost everyone guesses Spain; its real birthplace is a holiday home on the Pacific coast of Mexico.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Enrique Corcuera invented padel in 1969 in Acapulco, Mexico, and reports no competing origin claim.

explanation: Enrique Corcuera built the first walled court in Acapulco, and a Spanish friend took the idea home to Marbella, which is how Spain became its heartland.

question: Which tennis player won the French Open men's singles title a record fourteen times, more than most all-time greats have won across all four Grand Slams combined?
source_excerpt: Nadal won 92 ATP Tour singles titles, with 22 major titles—including a record 14 French Open titles.

extra.why_interesting: The sheer number is the hook: fourteen titles at a single Grand Slam is more than most all-time greats win in total across all four.
extra.verification_notes: Nadal's record 14 French Open men's singles titles is confirmed by Wikipedia, and nothing found suggests it has been matched or surpassed.

explanation: Nadal lost only four matches in his entire career at Roland Garros, and his statue now stands at the entrance to the grounds.

question: Both are the oldest championships in their sports. Which one was held first: the Wimbledon tennis championships, or golf's Open Championship?
source_excerpt: The first Open Championship took place on October 17, 1860 at Prestwick Golf Club in Scotland.

extra.why_interesting: Wimbledon's heavy tradition makes it feel like the ancient one, but golf's Open had already been running for seventeen years when the first Wimbledon was played.
extra.verification_notes: The first Open Championship was held in 1860 at Prestwick, 17 years before the first Wimbledon in 1877 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Championship).
